notes.meaning: When the crowd came to arrest Jesus, Peter quickly drew a sword and cut off the ear of the high priest's servant, named Malchus. Peter acted out of bold loyalty, but he struck rashly without waiting for Jesus' permission. Jesus did not want physical violence, and the other Gospels show that He immediately healed the wounded man.

Jesus commanded Peter to put away his sword, warning that those who live by violence will die by violence. Christ's spiritual kingdom does not advance through weapons of war, nor should private individuals take the law into their own hands. Peter was also putting his own life in grave danger by attacking an armed troop alone.

differ.view: Magistrates lawfully hold the sword from God to punish evildoers, but private citizens are forbidden from taking up weapons for personal revenge or violent defense.
Christ's religion must never be defended by government force or worldly weapons, and private believers must not resist civil officers even when treated unjustly.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars question whether Jesus spoke these exact words here, viewing them as drawn from a similar proverb found in Revelation 13:10.

notes.meaning: Jesus reminded Peter that He did not need human defense, because His Father stood ready to send more than twelve legions of mighty angels at a single word. A Roman legion had thousands of soldiers, so this vast army would easily overpower any earthly mob. Jesus was not a helpless victim; He was choosing to lay down His life willingly.

If Jesus called down legions of angels to save Himself from arrest, the ancient prophecies about the suffering Messiah could never come true. The Old Testament foretold that the Lamb of God must suffer and die to carry out God's plan of salvation. Jesus submitted peacefully because His deepest desire was to obey the written word of God.

Jesus asked the crowd why they came secretly at night with weapons as if He were a dangerous, violent criminal hiding from justice. He pointed out that He had taught openly in the temple courtyards every day where they could have arrested Him without any fight. Their cowardly night raid exposed their guilty consciences and unjust hatred.

All these distressing events happened so that the writings of the prophets concerning Christ's suffering would be fulfilled. Terrified by the sight of armed guards and seeing that Jesus surrendered without fighting, every single disciple abandoned Him and ran away into the dark. Even their shameful flight fulfilled Scripture, leaving Jesus to tread the path of suffering entirely alone.

The armed band took Jesus directly to the palace of Caiaphas the high priest, where the national council of religious leaders had gathered in the middle of the night. These rulers and scribes were filled with bitter hatred and had plotted beforehand to destroy Him. Instead of finding justice in this court, Jesus faced an illegal assembly bent on His death.

Peter loved Jesus enough to follow Him, but fear made him keep his distance so he would not be noticed. He slipped into the open courtyard and sat by the fire among the temple guards and servants just to see how the trial would turn out. Following at a distance and joining worldly company placed Peter in a dangerous spot of temptation.

The religious rulers had already decided to execute Jesus, but they needed charges that would give their verdict an appearance of fairness. They actively searched for people willing to give false testimony against Him. Rather than acting as honest judges seeking the truth, they became corrupt prosecutors trying to invent an excuse to put Him to death.

Many false witnesses came forward, but their stories were so inconsistent and full of contradictions that none of the charges could hold up under the law. Finally, two men came forward and claimed Jesus had bragged that He could tear down the temple of God and build it again in three days. This twisted what Jesus actually meant when He spoke years before about the temple of His own body rising from the dead.

Frustrated that the witnesses were failing to make a solid case, the high priest stood up to pressure Jesus directly. He demanded to know why Jesus remained silent and had no defense against the allegations. Caiaphas hoped to bait Jesus into an angry or careless remark that could be turned into a crime.

Jesus kept silent because the charges were worthless and He was willing to be led like a quiet lamb to the slaughter. In desperation, Caiaphas placed Jesus under a solemn oath before the living God, commanding Him to say whether He was the Christ, the divine Son of God. Silence now would look like a denial of His true identity and mission, so the moment called for a clear answer.

Jesus replied plainly that He was indeed the Christ, using a common Jewish way of saying yes. He then warned the court that one day they would see Him sitting in divine majesty at the right hand of God and returning in power on the clouds of heaven. Though He was now standing bound as a prisoner before earthly judges, He announced that He would one day be their supreme Judge.

differ.view: The phrase hereafter pointed to Christ's impending exaltation through Pentecost, the rapid spread of the gospel, and the coming destruction of Jerusalem.
The word hereafter clearly separates Christ's humble first appearance on earth from His glorious second coming on the final day of judgment.

notes.meaning: Upon hearing this, Caiaphas ripped his robes as an outward sign of horror, shouting that Jesus had committed blasphemy by claiming divine authority. He told the council that they no longer needed any witnesses because they had heard the insult against God from Jesus' own lips. Caiaphas put on a show of religious outrage to cover up his own wicked scheme.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church fathers saw the high priest ripping his garments as a symbol that the Old Covenant priesthood was being torn apart and brought to an end.

notes.meaning: Caiaphas asked the council for their formal verdict, and they promptly declared that Jesus was guilty of a crime that deserved death. Blasphemy was punishable by execution under Jewish law, though the leaders still needed Roman approval to carry out a death sentence. By condemning the innocent Lord of glory, they displayed the deep corruption of their own hearts.

The men holding Jesus began to abuse Him with vicious cruelty, spitting in His holy face, punching Him, and slapping Him with open hands. Other Gospels note that they blindfolded Him and sneered, asking Him to prophesy who had struck Him. Through all of this painful mockery, Jesus endured the humiliation patiently to fulfill ancient Scripture and bear our shame.

While Jesus was being tried above, Peter sat in the open courtyard below trying to warm himself by the fire. A servant girl looked at him and said aloud that he had been with Jesus the Galilean. Caught off guard by fear, Peter immediately lied in front of everyone, pretending he did not even understand what she was talking about.

Feeling exposed, Peter moved away from the fire into the entrance porch, but another girl pointed him out to the bystanders as a follower of Jesus of Nazareth. To make his denial sound stronger, Peter swore an oath and insisted that he did not even know the man. His fear drove him deeper into sin, breaking his promises to stay loyal to his Master.

About an hour later, the people standing around came and told Peter that his northern Galilean accent proved he was one of Jesus' followers. In total panic, Peter began calling down curses on himself and swearing that he had no idea who Jesus was. The very moment those words left his mouth, a rooster crowed in the early morning darkness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters suggest Matthew presents Peter here as an outright apostate and false disciple rather than merely a believer failing under pressure.

notes.meaning: The crow of the rooster pierced Peter's conscience, bringing back Jesus' warning that he would deny Him three times before the bird crowed. Stricken with deep grief over his failure and weakness, Peter rushed outside into the night and wept bitter tears of genuine sorrow. Unlike Judas who fell into despair, Peter experienced true repentance that led to forgiveness and restoration.
